{"id": "94:7/q05", "question": "How is fanṣab read, and what changes with the variants?", "turns_on": "Whether altered consonant vocalization or doubling is a transmitted reading, and whether an omitted object supports a succession claim.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q05/p1", "position": "A doubled consonant reading gives the sense of pouring oneself wholly into another act, or, in one account, going home.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī connect the doubled form to inṣibāb; ALUSI-FULL describes a doubled open yāʾ, while others specify bāʾ. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī also report a doubled-bāʾ reading construed as heading to Medina or returning home after jihad, which they reject as a reading."}, {"id": "94:7/q05/p2", "position": "Fanṣib with kasra on ṣād is taken by some Imāmīs as 'appoint a successor,' especially ʿAlī.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and followers call the reading fabricated or anomalous and say hostile readers could force the root into hating ʿAlī. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says no recognized scholar attests it. Ibn al-ʿArabī denies the Prophet appointed a successor. Al-Ālūsī says no object is named: a Sunni could instead supply Abū Bakr, citing his leadership of prayer in the final illness; he questions the Ghadīr Khumm claim and objects to a pilgrimage setting because the sūra is Meccan, but rejects al-Zamakhsharī's hate-ʿAlī analogy as flawed. Some supply 'caliph' as omitted object."}, {"id": "94:7/q05/p3", "position": "The common imperative fanṣab has an ungeminated, still bāʾ and commands exertion.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls this the majority form; al-Samīn derives it from naṣaba."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q06", "question": "What does placing the completion clause first do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q06/p1", "position": "It prepares the main command and emphasizes doing a new task in sequence after each completed one.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says fanṣab is the main command and the initial time clause sets its sequence; he calls the expression concise yet rich. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the future marker and paired fa particles also signal sequence and connection to what precedes."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q07", "question": "What is the force of the fa connecting the commands?", "turns_on": "Whether the fronted elements supply a conditional sense explaining fa.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q07/p1", "position": "The fa links actions because the fronted complements imply restriction and thus a conditional sense.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr adduces comparable Qurʾānic clauses (39:66, 74:3–5, 83:26, 10:58) and says this resolves al-Ṭībī's and Ibn al-Shajarī's puzzlement over fa with wāw."}, {"id": "94:7/q07/p2", "position": "The pairing of fa and wāw is syntactically astonishing.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭībī, citing Ibn al-Shajarī, finds it striking because fa usually coordinates, answers a condition, or accompanies a relative clause; Ibn ʿĀshūr disputes the difficulty."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q08", "question": "What transition does the verse command when one is free?", "turns_on": "Which task has ended, whether the omitted activity is general or specific, and what kind of effort follows.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q08/p1", "position": "After finishing prayer, exert yourself in supplication, petitioning God for your needs.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and others transmit the prayer-to-supplication sequence; al-Baghawī and al-Rāzī add that God answers. Al-Nasafī notes disagreement over whether this is before or after salām. Ibn Masʿūd glosses exertion as supplication. Some specify the prescribed prayer and some the tashahhud."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p2", "position": "After finishing worldly or personal affairs, turn to prayer and worship with undivided intention.", "reasons": "Mujāhid repeatedly gives this reading. Ibn Kathīr cites reports against praying while food is served or while resisting bodily needs, supporting an undistracted mind. Al-Ālūsī says ordinary farāgh often means freedom from worldly occupations but judges this reading weakest in context because of fa; al-Ṭabarī includes it as one example of the general command."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p3", "position": "After finishing jihad or a military campaign, devote yourself to worship.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Zayd ibn Aslam give this sequence. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Jishumī object that the sūra is Meccan and jihad was prescribed in Medina. Al-Ālūsī notes possible replies: a Medinan sūra or verse, or a delayed ruling. Al-Biqāʿī associates relief from the Arab campaign with year eight after Hijra."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p4", "position": "After completing prescribed worship, take up voluntary worship, especially night prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd often specifies the night vigil; other reports give voluntary good works generally. Ibn ʿAbbās is also cited for moving from an obligatory act to encouraged good works."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p5", "position": "After any significant completed duty, undertake another act of worship or other important work, leaving no idle gap.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī grounds the unrestricted scope in the unqualified condition; al-Ālūsī cites the causal fa and treats named devotions as examples. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the omitted object generically as the Prophet's important duties, prioritized when they overlap; he cites prayer amid combat (4:102–103). Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, and al-Nasafī stress continuous worship and gratitude for past and promised favors. Al-Biqāʿī lists glorification, seeking forgiveness, and voluntary prayer. Elmalılı includes renewed effort after ease and rest."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p6", "position": "After the prayer's bowing and prostration or tashahhud, supplicate while seated before the salutation.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Masʿūd place petition within the final sitting; the latter says prayer is complete after bowing and prostration even if ritual impurity then occurs. Al-Shaʿbī and al-Zuhrī allow petitions for worldly and afterlife needs after tashahhud. Al-Aṣamm also directs supplication after bowing, prostration, and recitation."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p7", "position": "After conveying revelation or calling people, devote yourself to worship in gratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī ties worship to past blessings and promised favors; al-Nasafī specifically says to move from calling people to worship. Al-Biqāʿī allows the demanding reception of revelation as the completed task."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p8", "position": "On rising to pray, exert yourself in presenting your need to God.", "reasons": "Mujāhid's formulation locates the effort at the start of prayer rather than after its completion; Ibn Kathīr also transmits a version about striving for one's need upon beginning prayer."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p9", "position": "After delivering the message, seek forgiveness for the Prophet and believers.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī identifies the completed work as conveying revelation and the new labor as seeking forgiveness for himself and believing men and women; al-Jishumī also urges turning to God in every religious and worldly need."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p10", "position": "After tending to people or creation, turn to worship of God.", "reasons": "Al-Qāsim, Junayd, and others cast the movement as withdrawing from people's affairs into devotion to the Real; Qutb includes detachment and aspiration."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p11", "position": "After conveying the mission, seek intercession.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ and other transmitters name intercession as the subsequent labor, sometimes after worship rather than after delivery of the message."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p12", "position": "After fulfilling a duty, devote health and spare time to worship.", "reasons": "ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa and Abū ʿIyāḍ invoke the value of health and free time; Shurayḥ's rebuke of wrestlers illustrates waste of the opportunity."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p13", "position": "After finishing enemy jihad, struggle against the self.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī transmit this sequence; the cited saying about return from lesser to greater jihad illustrates it, though al-Ālūsī questions its chronological fit with a Meccan sūra."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p14", "position": "After worship, turn inward with the heart or seek forgiveness in fear that worship may be rejected.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī contrasts outward worship with inward devotion; al-Thaʿlabī's anonymous view urges shame and repentance for imperfect worship."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p15", "position": "After delivering the message, fight the enemy.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī raises this as an additional possibility; al-Jishumī rejects making jihad the command because the sūra is Meccan and jihad had not begun."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p16", "position": "When alone or inwardly free of prophetic duties, remember and worship God.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim glosses farāgh as solitude and naṣb as exertion; another report makes a heart free of messenger duties the occasion for remembrance. Jaʿfar says to be free of all besides God."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p17", "position": "After completing the given work, direct oneself wholly to another worship.", "reasons": "Some read a doubled consonant in fanṣab and derive it from inṣibāb, a pouring or complete turning toward the new devotion; al-Ālūsī uses this sense."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p18", "position": "After completing the divine journey, return to steadfast work inviting people.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī describes a journey through, with, and from God before renewed outward invitation."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p19", "position": "After relief from constriction, take up the burdens of the prophetic message.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ ties the completion to relief from distress and the opening, lightening of burden, and raising of renown in 94:1–4; she calls this the best specification if one is needed."}, {"id": "94:7/q08/p20", "position": "After one hardship, endure another while seeking two eases and closeness to God.", "reasons": "ʿIṣām al-Dīn derives this from the preceding promise

{"id": "94:7/q09", "question": "How does this command relate to the preceding favors and promise of ease?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q09/p1", "position": "God's past favors and promised future relief call for grateful, persistent worship and renewed work.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, and others see the injunction as gratitude. Al-Biqāʿī adds gratitude brings increase; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 14:7 and reads 94:5–6 as encouraging endurance of the mission. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ and Corpus Coranicum trace a contrast between finishing and exerting after hardship and ease; Elmalılı says each ease should spur further progress."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q10", "question": "What does the command teach about idle time and recreation?", "turns_on": "Whether the injunction to avoid idle time excludes permitted leisure and festival recreation.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q10/p1", "position": "Free time should be used for worship or useful worldly and religious work; pointless idleness is censured.", "reasons": "Shurayḥ rebukes wrestlers in many accounts; al-Shaʿbī censures a man moving stones. ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd dislike a person with neither worldly nor afterlife work. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Ālūsī call useless idleness foolish or heedless. Al-Nuḥḥās extends the point to any completed work."}, {"id": "94:7/q10/p2", "position": "Ordinary people need not work without pause; festival play and song are permitted.", "reasons": "Ibn al-ʿArabī challenges Shurayḥ's objection to festival play: Abyssinians performed with shields and spears before the Prophet in the mosque, and the Prophet told Abū Bakr to let two girls sing on Eid. Al-Qurṭubī says uninterrupted application is disliked for ordinary people."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q11", "question": "What did Shurayḥ and others say on seeing idle people?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported incident concerns wrestling, pointless carrying, general idleness, or festival play.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q11/p1", "position": "Shurayḥ rebuked two men wrestling and invoked this verse.", "reasons": "The versions differ only in whether he says the command calls for worship, effort, or turning to God; one later report attributes a similar rebuke to Sharīk."}, {"id": "94:7/q11/p2", "position": "ʿUmar or Ibn Masʿūd disliked seeing anyone idle in both worldly and afterlife work.", "reasons": "The attribution varies between sources: al-Naḥḥās gives Ibn Masʿūd; al-Kashshāf and al-Ālūsī give ʿUmar."}, {"id": "94:7/q11/p3", "position": "Al-Shaʿbī rebuked a man carrying or moving stones as a misuse of free time.", "reasons": "The Kashshāf versions link the anecdote to the view that pointless activity reflects poor judgment."}, {"id": "94:7/q11/p4", "position": "A report has Shurayḥ objecting to festival play, but Ibn al-ʿArabī challenges the objection.", "reasons": "Ibn al-ʿArabī cites the Prophet watching Abyssinian spear and shield play and permitting two girls to sing on Eid."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q12", "question": "When may the prayer's concluding supplication be made?", "turns_on": "Whether 'finishing prayer' includes the final sitting before salām or follows the salām.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q12/p1", "position": "Before the salām, after the bowing, prostration, or tashahhud, while still seated.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Masʿūd, al-Shaʿbī, and al-Zuhrī are cited. Ibn Masʿūd holds that bowing and prostrations complete prayer even if ritual impurity then occurs, leaving room to ask God while seated. Al-Aṣamm also directs supplication after bowing, prostration, and recitation."}, {"id": "94:7/q12/p2", "position": "After finishing the prayer and salām.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī records that some authorities place the supplication after salutation; many reports say simply 'after prayer' without deciding the exact moment."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q13", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from the command?", "turns_on": "Whether free time denotes outward completion, inward emptying, or the end of a spiritual journey.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q13/p1", "position": "After the outward obligatory prayer, return beyond the natural self to a solitary secret station with God.", "reasons": "Al-Tustarī relates this to the Prophet's reported intimate time with God that admits no other."}, {"id": "94:7/q13/p2", "position": "When free of everything besides God, remember Him.", "reasons": "Jaʿfar's reported saying makes inward freedom the condition for remembrance."}, {"id": "94:7/q13/p3", "position": "After worship of the self, devote the heart inwardly.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī reports this as another way to understand the move from one work to the next."}, {"id": "94:7/q13/p4", "position": "After the inward journey through, with, and from God, turn outward in steadfast invitation.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī sees an inward journey preceding renewed work among people."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q14", "question": "What reports illustrate moving from one demand to another?", "turns_on": "Which reported circumstance—campaign, prayer distractions, or travel—illustrates completion and renewed action.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q14/p1", "position": "The Prophet is reported to call return from a campaign a move from lesser jihad to greater jihad.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr uses the saying as an example of following one task with another. Al-Ālūsī notes its use for struggle against the self, while raising the Meccan chronology issue."}, {"id": "94:7/q14/p2", "position": "Reports about food and bodily need counsel clearing distractions before prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites a report from ʿĀʾisha that prayer should not be begun with food present or while resisting bodily needs; Muslim transmits it and the fuller source calls it sound. Another report says to begin with dinner when it is served at the prayer call, transmitted by al-Bukhārī."}, {"id": "94:7/q14/p3", "position": "Travel is a piece of torment, so after one's need is done one should hurry back to family.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn al-ʿArabī cite this Prophetic report to support the meaning of returning home, while rejecting a fabricated doubled-bāʾ reading used to claim it."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q15", "question": "What does the Bedouin's word lesson distinguish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q15/p1", "position": "An opening in a wall or stick has ḍamma, while an opening from distress has fatḥa.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ says he heard this after fleeing al-Ḥajjāj and listening to verses that patience lifts sorrow; a messenger then announced al-Ḥajjāj's death. The distinction pleased him."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q16", "question": "How should someone respond after completing the Qurʾān?", "turns_on": "Whether the notes concern a prescribed practice at completion or reported benefits of completion.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q16/p1", "position": "Supplicate at the completion, often with raised hands in tarāwīḥ before bowing.", "reasons": "Aḥmad recommends completing in tarāwīḥ and praying before the bow with raised hands, including for those present; al-Faḍl reports practicing this with Aḥmad behind him. Makkans, Basrans, Medinans, and reports from ʿUthmān attest similar practice. Al-Nawawī strongly urges comprehensive prayers for the afterlife, Muslims, and leaders."}, {"id": "94:7/q16/p2", "position": "Gather family and others at a completion.", "reasons": "Anas gathered family and neighbors; Qatāda reports Ibn ʿAbbās arranging watchers so he could witness a man's completion."}, {"id": "94:7/q16/p3", "position": "The completion brings mercy, an answered supplication, or an angel's kiss.", "reasons": "Ḥabīb ibn Abī ʿAmra relates the angel's kiss, approved by Aḥmad; Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid report answered supplication, and Mujāhid also reports descending mercy. Al-Bukhārī reportedly completed frequently in Ramadan and spoke of answered supplication."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q17", "question": "Who should lead supplication at a Qurʾān completion?", "turns_on": "Whether the completing reader or a respected leader voices the prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q17/p1", "position": "The reader who completed the Qurʾān should supplicate.", "reasons": "Some teachers of Ibn al-Jazarī prefer this arrangement."}, {"id": "94:7/q17/p2", "position": "A shaykh or someone sought for blessing should supplicate.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī says most scholars he knew followed this practice; he accepts either because the one supplicating and the one saying amen share in the prayer, illustrated by Moses and Aaron in 10:89."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q18", "question": "Does adding a letter necessarily make a recitation preferable?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q18/p1", "position": "No; Aḥmad would not choose a form merely for an extra letter.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī rejects Ibn Mufliḥ's distinction between letter names and sounds as his own elaboration rather than Aḥmad's reason."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q19", "question": "How does arrangement of meaning govern spoken wording?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q19/p1", "position": "Meanings are arranged in the mind, and words take their places as their expressions.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī compares composition to building, linking, weaving, embroidery, engraving, and craft; ordinary speech may not say meanings are composed, yet these analogies concern meaning-relations, not words alone. A word's location depends on its meaning."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q20", "question": "How does this command lead into the following call to desire God?", "turns_on": "Whether the next clause directs the worshipper's own desire or, in a variant, urges others.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q20/p1", "position": "Work should be directed to God alone, with sincere desire and requests for religious and worldly needs.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr stresses an undistracted mind and intention, al-Jishumī says to turn to God in every circumstance,

and Elmalılı relates labor for God's sake to reaching Him and to deeds being judged by intentions. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the conjunction completes the movement from distress through ease to exclusive longing for God."}, {"id": "94:7/q20/p2", "position": "A reported variant of the next imperative, faraghib, means urge others toward what God has.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes it to Zayd ibn ʿAlī and Ibn Abī ʿAbla; it is from the doubled verb raghiba."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q21", "question": "How is 'desire' construed in the following verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q21/p1", "position": "Raghiba normally takes the desired object with fī, the one petitioned directly, and an for turning away.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites ʿĀʾisha's reading of an omitted preposition as an in 4:127."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q22", "question": "Are al-Ḍuḥā and al-Sharḥ one sūra or two?", "turns_on": "Whether prayer recitation without a second basmala outweighs the transmitted separation by basmala.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q22/p1", "position": "They form one sūra, or were recited together without a second basmala.", "reasons": "Asad reports Ṭāwūs and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz treating them as one in prayer, citing al-Rāzī; Study Quran reports a similar explanation involving Companions."}, {"id": "94:7/q22/p2", "position": "They are two sūras.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī rejects unity because the basmala separates them and transmitted agreement establishes two."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q23", "question": "How do al-Ḍuḥā and al-Sharḥ relate in sequence and theme?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q23/p1", "position": "Al-Sharḥ follows and continues al-Ḍuḥā's reassurance, moving from blessings and hardship to renewed striving.", "reasons": "Asad says the revelation followed almost immediately. Islāḥī says al-Ḍuḥā covers shelter and early favors whereas al-Sharḥ addresses blessings after Islam spread, with promised success beginning to materialize. Study Quran distinguishes external needs in 93 from spiritual relief in 94. The address reaches the Prophet and, through him, believers."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q24", "question": "Where and when was the sūra revealed?", "turns_on": "Whether the commonly accepted Makkan setting permits a literal post-jihad command, or later dating or delayed application is possible.", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q24/p1", "position": "It is Makkan, commonly placed just after Sūra 93.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports the majority view. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Jishumī use the Makkan date to object to interpretations based on later jihad; al-Ālūsī notes the same issue."}, {"id": "94:7/q24/p2", "position": "The whole sūra is Madinan, or only verses 5–6 are Madinan.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports Ibn ʿAbbās for the whole sūra and an unnamed view for verses 5–6; al-Ālūsī mentions Medinan dating or a delayed ruling as possible answers to the jihad chronology objection."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q25", "question": "What merit is reported for reciting al-Sharḥ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q25/p1", "position": "Reciting it is likened to visiting the distressed Prophet and relieving him.", "reasons": "The report appears in al-Kashshāf and al-Bayḍāwī without a grade in these notes."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q26", "question": "What warning do the sources give about invented readings or reports?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q26/p1", "position": "A sound meaning must not be attached to a self-invented reading or hadith as if it were revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn al-ʿArabī say this lies about God and the Messenger; the fuller note invokes 2:281. The doubled reading about returning from travel illustrates the distinction between a supported meaning and an invalid reading."}]}
{"id": "94:7/q27", "question": "What broad maxims does the sūra's ending teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:7/q27/p1", "position": "Hardship yields ease; effort and reward correspond; intention gives work its direction.", "reasons": "Elmalılı articulates these maxims and says labor for God's sake leads one to God. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes the assurance of accompanying ease as what keeps people from perishing under hardship."}]}
{"id": "94:8/q01", "question": "Who is “your Lord” here, and why seek Him?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:8/q01/p1", "position": "God, the giver of the favors recalled in these two sūras and the sole source of effective help.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī identifies the Lord with the one who nurtured the Prophet through the favors already named, and says all creaturely power comes from Him. Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī say only He can grant a request."}]}
{"id": "94:8/q02", "question": "What does raghaba mean in this wording?", "turns_on": "The preposition changes whether desire moves toward or away from its object.", "positions": [{"id": "94:8/q02/p1", "position": "To desire, incline strongly toward, and earnestly seek what is loved.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes the Qurʾānic use for strong inclination outside religious contexts. Ibn ʿĀshūr defines raghbah as seeking attainment of a loved thing. Bursevī says raghaba fīhi or ilayhi is desiring and earnestly seeking."}, {"id": "94:8/q02/p2", "position": "With ʿan, raghaba means to turn desire away.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 4:127 and ʿĀʾisha's explanation, which supplies an omitted ʿan; Bursevī contrasts raghaba ʿanhu with the positive constructions."}]}
{"id": "94:8/q03", "question": "Why does the verb take ilā here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:8/q03/p1", "position": "It incorporates a sense of turning or approaching the one who possesses the desired thing.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the person sought usually takes the direct object and the desired thing fī; ilā evokes travel toward a destination, with Abraham's words in 37:99 as a comparison."}]}
{"id": "94:8/q04", "question": "Why is “to your Lord” placed before the verb?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:8/q04/p1", "position": "The fronting restricts desire to God alone.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says this makes hope exclusively divine and effort continuous. {"id": "94:8/q05", "question": "What is left unspoken as the object of desire?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "94:8/q05/p1", "position": "The omitted object embraces everything the Prophet may seek.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr names spiritual perfection, the spread of religion, and Muslim victory; al-Rāzī similarly includes religious and worldly needs and victory."}]}

Elmalılı describes an interval of excusable ignorance; al-Ālūsī rejects the destruction gloss."}, {"id": "98:1/q12/p5", "position": "They had not yet divided over Muhammad; his mission split them into believers and deniers.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī favors intransitive separation and says they formerly agreed he was a prophet; Ibn ʿĪsā says they agreed God would send a messenger."}, {"id": "98:1/q12/p6", "position": "They were under God's power and care, not abandoned or condemned before warning arrived.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya favors a warner establishing proof and completing blessing; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 9:115; Asad cites 6:131–132, 17:15 and 42:13."}, {"id": "98:1/q12/p7", "position": "The Prophet's arrival unsettled certainty in inherited religions.", "reasons": "Rāzī compares 2:213; Elmalılı distinguishes infikāk as detachment from later dispersion; al-Ālūsī finds this unsatisfactory."}, {"id": "98:1/q12/p8", "position": "They continued praising Muhammad until his arrival, then spoke falsely about him.", "reasons": "Rāzī links 2:89; al-Ālūsī objects that this supplies an unstated complement."}, {"id": "98:1/q12/p9", "position": "The groups remained in mutual acceptance, then parted from each other.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says each accepted the other's belief; al-Ālūsī objects that a proof should unite them."}, {"id": "98:1/q12/p10", "position": "They would remain unbelievers even if the proof came.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Jabbār reads ḥattā conditionally; Rāzī and Elmalılı object that Arabic ḥattā does not bear this meaning."}, {"id": "98:1/q12/p11", "position": "Obstinate deniers demanded yet further signs although they knew the truth.", "reasons": "Jishumī cites 4:153; Islāḥī says they demanded an angel or separate pages, comparing 74:52."}, {"id": "98:1/q12/p12", "position": "They held their religion outwardly until the Messenger's pages showed its abrogation.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī calls this weak."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q13", "question": "Why did the verse seem difficult beside 98:4?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q13/p1", "position": "On an apparent reading, 'until' implies departure from disbelief upon proof, but 98:4 and subsequent history show rejection.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī calls the passage exceptionally difficult; Ibn ʿĀshūr adds that a subjunctive seems to put an already arrived messenger in the future. {"id": "98:1/q14", "question": "What time and attachment does ḥattā taʾtiyahum express?", "turns_on": "Whether its imperfect is historical, reported speech, or habitual.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q14/p1", "position": "The imperfect can refer to an arrival already past or recall their earlier future expectation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿArafa compares 2:102; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the remainder was not yet narrated as past. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it reproduces their earlier claim."}, {"id": "98:1/q14/p2", "position": "The until phrase attaches to munfakkīn, though attachment to lam yakun is also reported.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives both; al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı choose munfakkīn."}, {"id": "98:1/q14/p3", "position": "The imperfect can portray recurring clarification or a disposition across past, present and future.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī links it to repeated messengers and recitation and to unstable religious changes."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q15", "question": "What does bayyina mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q15/p1", "position": "A manifest proof or testimony that distinguishes truth from falsehood.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī and Ṭabrisī connect its root to separation; Prophet, fair witness or any proof can bear the name. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads its feminine form as a sign or testimony and connects Matthew's 'testimony to all nations'."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q16", "question": "What is the clear proof?", "turns_on": "Whether Muhammad, Qurʾān, both, or an awaited extraordinary sign.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q16/p1", "position": "Muhammad himself, whose character and miracles establish his mission.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jurayj name him; Rāzī adduces his unfeigned resolve, miraculous qualities and signs, citing 33:46, al-Jāḥiẓ and al-Ghazālī."}, {"id": "98:1/q16/p2", "position": "The Qurʾān, which makes truth clear.", "reasons": "Qatāda and Ibn Zayd say so; Rāzī cites 20:133 and proposes an omitted noun before the ensuing messenger."}, {"id": "98:1/q16/p3", "position": "Muhammad together with Qurʾān or the revealed books and his signs.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī mentions the Messenger's miraculous character and Qurʾān's silencing challengers; Biqāʿī includes Torah, Gospel and Psalms."}, {"id": "98:1/q16/p4", "position": "Messengers or proofs sent broadly, including earlier revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Rabīʿ says messengers; Abū Muslim cites demands for heavenly pages in 4:153 and 74:52."}, {"id": "98:1/q16/p5", "position": "The demanded extraordinary sign or miracle.", "reasons": "Islāḥī cites demands for an angel, heavenly book and separate pages; Ibn ʿĀshūr recounts earlier expected signs."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q17", "question": "What does the definite article in al-bayyina suggest?", "turns_on": "Whether a specific promised sign, generic kind, or magnification.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q17/p1", "position": "The expected Prophet or a magnified proof is intended.", "reasons": "Rāzī connects Torah and Gospel and the exceptional indefinite rasūl; Burṣawī stresses fulfillment of scriptural promises."}, {"id": "98:1/q17/p2", "position": "It can be a generic mental definite, meaning a known kind of proof.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 'enter the market' and Zuhayr's generic 'war'; rhetoricians allow indefinite meaning."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q18", "question": "How does the next verse's 'a messenger' explain the proof?", "turns_on": "Whether it is apposition, an independent nominative, or accusative circumstance.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q18/p1", "position": "The indefinite messenger is apposition or explanatory replacement of the definite proof.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī cites 85:15–16; Elmalılı also permits an omitted explanatory subject and predicate."}, {"id": "98:1/q18/p2", "position": "Rasūlan can be accusative as a circumstance.", "reasons": "Ubayy's and ʿAbd Allāh's variants support this parse."}, {"id": "98:1/q18/p3", "position": "The messenger begins a fresh nominative clause.", "reasons": "Farrāʾ distinguishes the indefinite from the definite proof."}]}
{"id": "98:1/q19", "question": "How does the sūra connect to revelation and state its overall purpose?", "turns_on": "Whether the link centers on descent, demand for proof, or the period before a messenger.", "positions": [{"id": "98:1/q19/p1", "position": "It follows the preceding account of revelation by explaining the clear proof's arrival and reception.", "reasons": "Jishumī links al-Qadr; Abū Ḥayyān also invokes 96:1; Biqāʿī compares the blessed night ending at dawn; Ālūsī explains why Qurʾān was revealed."}, {"id": "98:1/q19/p2", "position": "It rebukes communities who awaited proof yet rejected it and contrasts believers' and deniers' fates.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr adds refutation of their claimed religious obligation, punishment and Qurʾān's superiority; Qutb names the final Messenger's necessity and simple core religion."}, {"id": "98:1/q19/p3", "position": "It explains the preprophetic interval and when proof establishes accountability.", "reasons": "Elmalılı cites 5:19 and 17:15; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 9:115."}]}
